Question:
Find the name and position of the head of the department with the least employees.
answer: SELECT T2.name ,  T2.position FROM department AS T1 JOIN physician AS T2 ON T1.head  =  T2.EmployeeID GROUP BY departmentID ORDER BY count(departmentID) LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the department records and assign the alias used to identify each department: `FROM department AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each department to its head physician by matching the department’s `head` value with the physician’s employee ID: `JOIN physician AS T2 ON T1.head = T2.EmployeeID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined records by department so the employee-count ordering can be evaluated for each department: `GROUP BY departmentID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort departments by their employee count in ascending order, placing the smallest count first: `ORDER BY count(departmentID)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the head physician’s name and position, and retain only the first department after sorting: `SELECT T2.name, T2.position` and `LIMIT 1`.

intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT count(departmentID) FROM department GROUP BY departmentID

intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T2.name ,  T2.position FROM department AS T1 JOIN physician AS T2 ON T1.head  =  T2.EmployeeID GROUP BY departmentID ORDER BY count(departmentID) LIMIT 1;

Question:
Which patients made more than one appointment? Tell me the name and phone number of these patients.
answer: SELECT name ,  phone FROM appointment AS T1 JOIN patient AS T2 ON T1.patient  =  T2.ssn GROUP BY T1.patient HAVING count(*)  >  1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the appointment records, since each row represents an appointment that contributes to a patient's total: `FROM appointment AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each appointment to its patient record by matching the appointment's patient identifier to the patient's SSN: `JOIN patient AS T2 ON T1.patient = T2.ssn`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Collect all appointment rows belonging to the same patient into one group: `GROUP BY T1.patient`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Retain only patient groups containing more than one appointment: `HAVING count(*) > 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the requested patient details from the joined patient table by placing this clause at the beginning: `SELECT name, phone`.

Question:
Which physicians have never taken any appointment? Find their names.
answer: SELECT name FROM physician EXCEPT SELECT T2.name FROM appointment AS T1 JOIN physician AS T2 ON T1.Physician  =  T2.EmployeeID

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build the first result set containing every physician’s name: `SELECT name FROM physician`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: For the second result set, start from appointment records and alias the table for precise column references: `FROM appointment AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Link each appointment to the physician who handled it through the employee identifier: `JOIN physician AS T2 ON T1.Physician  =  T2.EmployeeID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Project the names of physicians represented in the joined appointment records: `SELECT T2.name`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Apply set difference between the complete physician-name set and the appointed-physician-name set by placing this operator between their SELECT statements: `EXCEPT`.

Question:
What are the name and primarily affiliated department name of each physician?
answer: SELECT T1.name ,  T3.name FROM physician AS T1 JOIN affiliated_with AS T2 ON T1.EmployeeID  =  T2.physician JOIN department AS T3 ON T2.department  =  T3.DepartmentID WHERE T2.PrimaryAffiliation  =  1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the physician records and assign the alias used to retrieve each physician's name: `FROM physician AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each physician to their affiliation record using the physician employee identifier: `JOIN affiliated_with AS T2 ON T1.EmployeeID = T2.physician`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Link the affiliation record to its department so the corresponding department name is available: `JOIN department AS T3 ON T2.department = T3.DepartmentID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the results to the physician's primary affiliation, represented by a value of 1: `WHERE T2.PrimaryAffiliation = 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project both requested values—the physician name and the primarily affiliated department name—in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T1.name, T3.name`.

Question:
What are the names of instructors who have taught C Programming courses?
answer: SELECT T1.name FROM instructor AS T1 JOIN teaches AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.id JOIN course AS T3 ON T2.course_id  =  T3.course_id WHERE T3.title  =  'C Programming'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the instructor table because it contains the names to be returned, and assign it the alias `T1`: `FROM instructor AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each instructor to their teaching assignments by matching the instructor ID in `instructor` and `teaches`: `JOIN teaches AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Link each teaching assignment to its course record so the course title can be examined: `JOIN course AS T3 ON T2.course_id = T3.course_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined records to assignments for the course whose title is exactly C Programming: `WHERE T3.title = 'C Programming'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the names of the instructors from alias `T1`, placing this clause before the accumulated joins and filter: `SELECT T1.name`.

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the advisor relationships, which connect each advised student to an instructor: `FROM advisor AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each advisor record to the corresponding instructor so their name and salary become available: `JOIN instructor AS T2 ON T1.i_id = T2.id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Join the advisor record to the advised student so the student's department can be checked: `JOIN student AS T3 ON T1.s_id = T3.id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the results to advisor relationships involving students in the Math department: `WHERE T3.dept_name = 'Math'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the requested instructor attributes from alias T2 by placing this clause before the joins and filter: `SELECT T2.name, T2.salary`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined rows to the course named Mobile Computing: `WHERE T2.title = 'Mobile Computing'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Project its prerequisite course identifier to complete the lookup subquery: `SELECT T1.prereq_id FROM prereq AS T1 JOIN course AS T2 ON T1.course_id = T2.course_id WHERE T2.title = 'Mobile Computing'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Use the prerequisite IDs to filter `course`, then project the requested prerequisite title with the outer clauses: `SELECT title FROM course WHERE course_id IN (...)`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Form one group per department so the professor rows can be counted department by department: `GROUP BY T1.dept_code`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the department groups by professor count in ascending order, then retain the group with the smallest count: `ORDER BY count(*) LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.hint_5: Count all city rows remaining after the join and country filter by using the projection: `SELECT count(*)`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Retain only country groups containing at least three city rows: `HAVING count(*) >= 3`.

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build the first result set by filtering payments whose amount is larger than 10: `FROM payment WHERE amount > 10`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Project the payment dates from this amount-based result set: `SELECT payment_date`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Combine this first result set with the staff-based result set while removing duplicate dates: `UNION`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: For the second result set, join each payment to its handling staff member and retain those whose first name is Elsa: `FROM payment AS T1 JOIN staff AS T2 ON T1.staff_id = T2.staff_id WHERE T2.first_name = 'Elsa'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the payment dates from the second, staff-filtered result set by placing this SELECT clause after the UNION: `SELECT T1.payment_date`.

Which film actor (actress) starred the most films? List his or her first name, last name and actor id.
answer: SELECT T2.first_name ,  T2.last_name ,  T2.actor_id FROM film_actor AS T1 JOIN actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id  =  T2.actor_id GROUP BY T2.actor_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the junction table because each row in `film_actor` represents an actor’s association with a film: `FROM film_actor AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the actor details to those film appearances using the shared actor identifier: `JOIN actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id = T2.actor_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one result group per actor so that each actor’s joined rows can be counted as film appearances: `GROUP BY T2.actor_id`.

prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the requested identity fields for the highest-ranked actor in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T2.first_name, T2.last_name, T2.actor_id`.

Which film actors (actresses) played a role in more than 30 films? List his or her first name and last name.
answer: SELECT T2.first_name ,  T2.last_name FROM film_actor AS T1 JOIN actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id  =  T2.actor_id GROUP BY T2.actor_id HAVING count(*)  >  30

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the junction table because each row in `film_actor` represents one actor's role in one film: `FROM film_actor AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each role record to the corresponding actor so the actor's name is available: `JOIN actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id = T2.actor_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Collect all role rows belonging to the same actor by grouping on the actor identifier: `GROUP BY T2.actor_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only actor groups containing more than 30 role records, which corresponds to appearing in more than 30 films: `HAVING count(*) > 30`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the first and last names of the qualifying actors in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T2.first_name, T2.last_name`.

Question:
Which customer, who has made at least one payment, has spent the least money? List his or her first name, last name, and the id.
answer: SELECT T1.first_name ,  T1.last_name ,  T1.customer_id FROM customer AS T1 JOIN payment AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id ORDER BY sum(amount) ASC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the customer table and assign the alias used for customer identity and name fields: `FROM customer AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each customer to their payment records; this also restricts the candidates to customers who have made at least one payment: `JOIN payment AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Combine all payment rows belonging to the same customer so their payment amounts can be aggregated: `GROUP BY T1.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the customer groups by total payment amount from least to greatest, then retain only the lowest-spending customer: `ORDER BY sum(amount) ASC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the requested first name, last name, and customer ID before the joined and grouped clauses: `SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name, T1.customer_id`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined rows to tracks whose genre name is Rock: `WHERE T1.Name = "Rock"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Calculate the mean of the matching tracks' unit prices using the aggregate expression: `AVG(T2.UnitPrice)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Place the average expression in the query's projection, then combine it with the genre source, track join, and Rock filter from the earlier steps: `SELECT AVG(T2.UnitPrice)`.

answer: SELECT T1.vehicle_id ,  T1.vehicle_details FROM Vehicles AS T1 JOIN Lessons AS T2 ON T1.vehicle_id  =  T2.vehicle_id GROUP BY T1.vehicle_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each vehicle to the lessons in which it was used by matching the shared vehicle identifier: `JOIN Lessons AS T2 ON T1.vehicle_id = T2.vehicle_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Combine lesson rows by vehicle so each vehicle's usage frequency can be evaluated: `GROUP BY T1.vehicle_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the grouped vehicles from most-used to least-used according to their lesson counts: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Keep only the top-ranked vehicle and project its ID and details using the clauses `LIMIT 1` and `SELECT T1.vehicle_id, T1.vehicle_details`.

Question:
What is average salary of the players in the team named 'Boston Red Stockings' ?
answer: SELECT avg(T1.salary) FROM salary AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  = 'Boston Red Stockings'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the salary records, since each row provides the player salary that will contribute to the requested average: `FROM salary AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Bring in team information so the salary rows can be associated with a team name: `JOIN team AS T2`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Match each salary record to the corresponding team using the identifiers specified by the target query: `ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined rows to the team whose name is Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate one average over the salaries remaining after the team filter by using the aggregate projection: `SELECT avg(T1.salary)`.

Question:
What are the first name, last name and id of the player with the most all star game experiences? Also list the count.
answer: SELECT T1.name_first , T1.name_last ,  T1.player_id ,   count(*) FROM player AS T1 JOIN all_star AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T1.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the player records and connect each player to their All-Star appearances through the shared player identifier: `FROM player AS T1 JOIN all_star AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group the joined appearance rows by player so that each player has one aggregated result: `GROUP BY T1.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Count the grouped All-Star records to measure each player's number of All-Star game experiences: `count(*)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank players from the highest appearance count to the lowest and retain only the top player: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the top player's first name, last name, identifier, and calculated appearance count: `SELECT T1.name_first, T1.name_last, T1.player_id, count(*)`.

Question:
In 2014, what are the id and rank of the team that has the largest average number of attendance?
answer: SELECT T2.team_id ,  T2.rank FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id WHERE T1.year  =  2014 GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T1.attendance) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from home-game attendance records and join each record to its team so the team's rank is available: `FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the attendance records to the requested year, 2014: `WHERE T1.year = 2014`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one result group per team so its average attendance can be calculated: `GROUP BY T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the team groups from highest to lowest average attendance and retain only the top team: `ORDER BY avg(T1.attendance) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the identifier and rank of the top-ranked result from the joined team table: `SELECT T2.team_id, T2.rank`.

Question:
What are the manager's first name, last name and id who won the most manager award?
answer: SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T2.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from player records so the manager's first and last names are available: `FROM player AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each player to their manager-award records using the shared player identifier: `JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the award records by manager so that each manager's rows can be counted together: `GROUP BY T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank managers by their number of award records from highest to lowest and retain the top result: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the top manager's first name, last name, and identifier in the requested order: `SELECT T1.name_first, T1.name_last, T2.player_id`.

Question:
Which 3 players won the most player awards? List their full name and id.
answer: SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T1.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T1.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the player records so each result can include the player's name and identifier: `FROM player AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each player to their award records using the shared player identifier: `JOIN player_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group all joined award rows by player so the number of rows in each group represents that player's award count: `GROUP BY T1.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank players by their award-row counts from highest to lowest and retain the top three: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project each qualifying player's first name, last name, and identifier in the result: `SELECT T1.name_first, T1.name_last, T1.player_id`.

Question:
What is the average height of the players from the college named 'Yale University'?
answer: SELECT avg(T1.height) FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_college AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id JOIN college AS T3 ON T3.college_id  = T2.college_id WHERE T3.name_full  =  'Yale University';

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the `player` table because the requested height values are stored in its `height` column: `FROM player AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each player to their college-attendance records using the shared player identifier: `JOIN player_college AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Join the attendance records to `college` so the associated institution can be identified by its full name: `JOIN college AS T3 ON T3.college_id = T2.college_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined rows to records associated with Yale University: `WHERE T3.name_full = 'Yale University'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the average of the qualifying players' heights by placing this aggregate projection before the assembled table and filtering clauses: `SELECT avg(T1.height)`.

Question:
What is the highest salary among each team? List the team name, id and maximum salary.
answer: SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id ,  max(T2.salary) FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id;

prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each team to its salary records using the shared `team_id`: `JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one result group for each team so its salary values can be aggregated: `GROUP BY T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Calculate the highest salary within each team’s group using the maximum aggregate: `max(T2.salary)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the team name, team ID, and calculated maximum salary in the requested order: `SELECT T1.name, T1.team_id, max(T2.salary)`.

intermediate_turns.question: What about for each team?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T1.name ,  avg(T2.salary) FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id;

intermediate_turns.question: Can you order the results by average salary?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T1.name ,  avg(T2.salary) FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T2.salary)

intermediate_turns.question: Please give the first one with its name and id.
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T2.salary) ASC LIMIT 1;

Question:
Find the players' first name and last name who won award both in 1960 and in 1961.
answer: SELECT T1.name_first , T1.name_last FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2 ON T1.Player_id = T2.Player_id WHERE T2.year  =  1960 INTERSECT SELECT T1.name_first , T1.name_last FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2 WHERE T2.year  =  1961

prefix_hints.hint_1: Project each qualifying player's first and last name from the `player` table: `SELECT T1.name_first , T1.name_last`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: For the first result set, join players to their award records using the shared player identifier: `FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2 ON T1.Player_id = T2.Player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the first result set to award records from 1960: `WHERE T2.year = 1960`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Use a set intersection and begin a second result set containing player names and award records: `INTERSECT SELECT T1.name_first , T1.name_last FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Restrict the second result set to 1961, so the intersection retains names appearing in both years: `WHERE T2.year = 1961`.

Question:
What are the name and id of the team with the most victories in 2008 postseason?
answer: SELECT T2.name ,  T1.team_id_winner FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008 GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from postseason series records and join each winning team identifier to the team table so its name can be retrieved: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the postseason results to the requested 2008 season: `WHERE T1.year = 2008`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the 2008 records by winning team so the number of postseason victories can be compared per team: `GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank teams by their grouped record count from greatest to least, then retain the top team: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the winning team's name and its postseason team identifier at the beginning of the assembled clauses: `SELECT T2.name, T1.team_id_winner`.

What is the number of wins the team Boston Red Stockings got in the postseasons each year in history?

prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each postseason winner to the corresponding team using the winner’s team ID and the team’s Baseball-Reference ID: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to postseason series won by the Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Group the qualifying postseason records by year so that a separate win count is calculated for each year: `GROUP BY T1.year`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the number of qualifying records alongside their postseason year: `SELECT count(*), T1.year`.

What is the total salary paid by team Boston Red Stockings in 2010?
answer: SELECT sum(T1.salary) FROM salary AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  = 'Boston Red Stockings' AND T1.year = 2010

prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each salary record to its team using the salary team identifier and the team's Baseball-Reference identifier: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the requested team name: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the year condition so that only salaries paid in 2010 are included: `AND T1.year = 2010`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the total of the qualifying salary amounts with the SUM aggregate in the projection: `SELECT sum(T1.salary)`.

Question:
What is the total home game attendance of team Boston Red Stockings from 2000 to 2010?
answer: SELECT sum(T1.attendance) FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' AND T1.year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2010;

prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each home-game record to its team information using the home-game team identifier and the team's Baseball Reference identifier: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the requested team by matching its full name: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the inclusive year range so attendance is counted from 2000 through 2010: `AND T1.year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2010`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the total attendance across all qualifying home-game records with the aggregate projection: `SELECT sum(T1.attendance)`.

Question:
List players' first name and last name who received salary from team Washington Nationals in both 2005 and 2007.
answer: SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals' INTERSECT SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2007 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the team named Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Limit the home-game records to the inclusive period from 1990 through 2000: `AND T1.year BETWEEN 1990 AND 2000`.

Question:

answer: SELECT T2.name FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year = 1980 ORDER BY T1.attendance ASC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the home-game records, where each team's yearly attendance is stored: `FROM home_game AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the team table to obtain the team's readable name, matching the home-game team identifier to the baseball-reference team identifier: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the home-game records to the requested season: `WHERE T1.year = 1980`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort attendance from smallest to largest so the least-attended team appears first: `ORDER BY T1.attendance ASC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the name of only the first team in that ordering by combining the projection and row limit around the earlier clauses: `SELECT T2.name` and `LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Show all the distinct product names with price higher than the average.
answer: SELECT DISTINCT Product_Name FROM PRODUCTS WHERE Product_Price  >  (SELECT avg(Product_Price) FROM PRODUCTS)

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the `PRODUCTS` table because it contains both the product names and their prices: `FROM PRODUCTS`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Calculate the average price across all products with a scalar aggregate subquery: `(SELECT avg(Product_Price) FROM PRODUCTS)`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Keep only products whose price is greater than the average returned by the subquery: `WHERE Product_Price > (SELECT avg(Product_Price) FROM PRODUCTS)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Project the product-name column for the qualifying products: `SELECT Product_Name`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Make the projected names unique by adding `DISTINCT` to the projection, then combine it with the source and filtering clauses: `SELECT DISTINCT Product_Name`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Link each order item to its corresponding product so its price can be evaluated: `JOIN Products AS T3 ON T2.Product_ID = T3.Product_ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined rows to products whose price is higher than 1000: `WHERE T3.Product_price > 1000`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the order date from the aliased orders table, placing this clause before the accumulated joins and filter: `SELECT T1.Order_Date`.

);

CREATE TABLE `Drama_Workshop_Groups` (
  `Workshop_Group_ID` NUMBER,

  `Currency_Code` TEXT,
  `Marketing_Region_Code` TEXT,
  `Store_Name` TEXT,
  `Store_Phone` TEXT,
  `Store_Email_Address` TEXT,
  `Other_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Workshop_Group_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Performers` (
  `Performer_ID` NUMBER,
  `Address_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Addresses`(`Address_ID`),
  `Customer_Name` TEXT,
  `Customer_Phone` TEXT,
  `Customer_Email_Address` TEXT,
  `Other_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Performer_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Customers` (
  `Customer_ID` TEXT,
  `Address_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Addresses`(`Address_ID`),
  `Customer_Name` TEXT,
  `Customer_Phone` TEXT,
  `Customer_Email_Address` TEXT,
  `Other_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Customer_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Stores` (
  `Store_ID` TEXT,
  `Address_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Addresses`(`Address_ID`),
  `Marketing_Region_Code` TEXT REFERENCES `Marketing_Regions`(`Marketing_Region_Code`),
  `Store_Name` TEXT,
  `Store_Phone` TEXT,
  `Store_Email_Address` TEXT,
  `Other_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Store_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Bookings` (
  `Booking_ID` NUMBER,
  `Customer_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Clients`(`Client_ID`),
  `Workshop_Group_ID` TEXT REFERENCES `Drama_Workshop_Groups`(`Workshop_Group_ID`),
  `Status_Code` TEXT,
  `Store_ID` NUMBER,
  `Order_Date` TIME,
  `Planned_Delivery_Date` TIME,
  `Actual_Delivery_Date` TIME,
  `Other_Order_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Booking_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Performers_in_Bookings` (
  `Order_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Bookings`(`Booking_ID`),
  `Performer_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Performers`(`Performer_ID`),
  PRIMARY KEY (`Order_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Customer_Orders` (
  `Order_ID` NUMBER,
  `Customer_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Customers`(`Customer_ID`),
  `Store_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Stores`(`Store_ID`),
  `Order_Date` TIME,
  `Planned_Delivery_Date` TIME,
  `Actual_Delivery_Date` TIME,
  `Other_Order_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Order_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Order_Items` (
  `Order_Item_ID` NUMBER,
  `Order_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Customer_Orders`(`Order_ID`),
  `Product_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Products`(`Product_ID`),
  `Order_Quantity` TEXT,
  `Other_Item_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Order_Item_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Invoices` (
  `Invoice_ID` NUMBER,
  `Order_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Customer_Orders`(`Order_ID`),
  `payment_method_code` TEXT REFERENCES `Ref_Payment_Methods`(`payment_method_code`),
  `Product_ID` NUMBER,
  `Order_Quantity` TEXT,
  `Other_Item_Details` TEXT,
  `Order_Item_ID` NUMBER,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Invoice_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Services` (
  `Service_ID` NUMBER,
  `Service_Type_Code` TEXT REFERENCES `Ref_Service_Types`(`Service_Type_Code`),
  `Workshop_Group_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Drama_Workshop_Groups`(`Workshop_Group_ID`),
  `Product_Description` TEXT,
  `Product_Name` TEXT,
  `Product_Price` NUMBER,
  `Other_Product_Service_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Service_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Bookings_Services` (
  `Order_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Bookings`(`Booking_ID`),
  `Product_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Services`(`Service_ID`),
  PRIMARY KEY (`Order_ID`)
);

CREATE TABLE `Invoice_Items` (
  `Invoice_Item_ID` NUMBER,
  `Invoice_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Invoices`(`Invoice_ID`),
  `Order_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Bookings_Services`(`Order_ID`),
  `Order_Item_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Order_Items`(`Order_Item_ID`),
  `Product_ID` NUMBER REFERENCES `Bookings_Services`(`Product_ID`),
  `Order_Quantity` NUMBER,
  `Other_Item_Details` TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Invoice_Item_ID`)

answer: SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the customer table, which contains the requested customer names: `FROM customers AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each customer to their orders through the shared `customer_id`: `JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by customer so that each group represents all orders placed by one customer: `GROUP BY T1.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank customers by their number of joined order rows in descending order, then retain only the largest group: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the name of the highest-ranked customer in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T1.customer_name`.

answer: SELECT T2.customer_name ,  count(*) FROM orders AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id GROUP BY T2.customer_id HAVING count(*)  >=  2

prefix_hints.hint_3: Count the order rows in each customer group to obtain the number of orders made: `count(*)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only customer groups whose order count is at least two: `HAVING count(*) >= 2`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project each qualifying customer's name together with the calculated order count: `SELECT T2.customer_name, count(*)`.

Question:
List the names of the customers who have once bought product "food".
answer: SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 JOIN order_items AS T3 JOIN products AS T4 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id AND T2.order_id = T3.order_id AND T3.product_id = T4.product_id WHERE T4.product_name = "food" GROUP BY T1.customer_id HAVING count(*)  >=  1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from customers and connect them to their orders using the customer identifier: `FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Continue through order items to products so each customer purchase can be associated with a product: `JOIN order_items AS T3 JOIN products AS T4 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id AND T2.order_id = T3.order_id AND T3.product_id = T4.product_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the purchase records to the product whose name is exactly "food": `WHERE T4.product_name = "food"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Group matching purchases by customer and retain customers with at least one such purchase: `GROUP BY T1.customer_id HAVING count(*) >= 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the customer name rather than the identifier by using this projection at the beginning of the assembled query: `SELECT T1.customer_name`.

answer: SELECT t1.resident_id ,  t1.other_details ,  count(*) FROM residents AS t1 JOIN residents_services AS t2 ON t1.resident_id  =  t2.resident_id GROUP BY t1.resident_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the resident records so each result can include the resident identifier and details: `FROM residents AS t1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each resident to their requested-service records using the shared resident identifier: `JOIN residents_services AS t2 ON t1.resident_id = t2.resident_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one result group per resident so the associated service requests can be counted: `GROUP BY t1.resident_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Return the resident ID, resident details, and number of joined request records for each group: `SELECT t1.resident_id, t1.other_details, count(*)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Sort the grouped results from the greatest number of service requests to the least: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC`.

Question:
What is the maximum number that a certain service is provided? List the service id, details and number.
answer: SELECT T1.service_id ,  T1.service_details ,  count(*) FROM Services AS T1 JOIN Residents_Services AS T2 ON T1.service_id  =  T2.service_id GROUP BY T1.service_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the service catalog and link each service to its provision records through the shared service identifier: `FROM Services AS T1 JOIN Residents_Services AS T2 ON T1.service_id = T2.service_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group the joined provision records by service so that each service receives its own count: `GROUP BY T1.service_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Count how many joined records belong to each service, representing the number of times it was provided: `count(*)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the grouped services from the highest provision count to the lowest and retain only the top one: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the winning service's identifier, details, and provision count in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T1.service_id, T1.service_details, count(*)`.

Question:
What are the id and details of the customers who have at least 3 events?
answer: SELECT T1.customer_id ,  T1.customer_details FROM Customers AS T1 JOIN Customer_Events AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id HAVING count(*)  >=  3

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the customer records, since the requested identifiers and details are stored in `Customers`: `FROM Customers AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each customer to their events using the shared customer identifier: `JOIN Customer_Events AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined event rows by customer so that each customer's events can be counted together: `GROUP BY T1.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Retain only customer groups containing at least three event rows: `HAVING count(*) >= 3`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project both the identifier and details for each qualifying customer: `SELECT T1.customer_id, T1.customer_details`.

Question:
Which events have the number of notes between one and three? List the event id and the property id.
answer: SELECT T1.Customer_Event_ID  ,  T1.property_id FROM Customer_Events AS T1 JOIN Customer_Event_Notes AS T2 ON T1.Customer_Event_ID  =  T2.Customer_Event_ID GROUP BY T1.customer_event_id HAVING count(*) BETWEEN 1 AND 3

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the customer event records and assign the alias used for their event and property identifiers: `FROM Customer_Events AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each event to its corresponding notes through the shared event identifier: `JOIN Customer_Event_Notes AS T2 ON T1.Customer_Event_ID = T2.Customer_Event_ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by event so that the number of associated notes can be calculated for each event: `GROUP BY T1.customer_event_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only event groups whose note count is inclusively between one and three: `HAVING count(*) BETWEEN 1 AND 3`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the requested event identifier and property identifier from the event table: `SELECT T1.Customer_Event_ID, T1.property_id`.

answer: SELECT DISTINCT T2.thing_id ,  T2.Type_of_Thing_Code FROM Timed_Status_of_Things AS T1 JOIN Things AS T2 ON T1.thing_id  =  T2.thing_id WHERE T1.Status_of_Thing_Code  =  'Close' OR T1.Date_and_Date  <  '2017-06-19 02:59:21'

answer: SELECT T1.customer_name ,  T1.customer_address FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id WHERE T2.order_status_code  =  "New" INTERSECT SELECT T1.customer_name ,  T1.customer_address FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id WHERE T2.order_status_code  =  "Pending"

answer: SELECT avg(total_amount_purchased) ,  avg(total_value_purchased) FROM Product_Suppliers WHERE supplier_id  =  (SELECT supplier_id FROM Product_Suppliers GROUP BY supplier_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1)

prefix_hints.hint_3: Return only the identifier of that top supplier by projecting `supplier_id` and limiting the ranked result to one row: `SELECT supplier_id FROM Product_Suppliers GROUP BY supplier_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Use the top-supplier query as a scalar subquery to retain only that supplier's purchase records: `FROM Product_Suppliers WHERE supplier_id = (SELECT supplier_id FROM Product_Suppliers GROUP BY supplier_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1)`.

Question:
Among all the claims, which settlements have a claimed amount that is no more than the average? List the claim start date.
answer: SELECT Date_Claim_Made FROM Claims WHERE Amount_Settled  <=  ( SELECT avg(Amount_Settled) FROM Claims )

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the `Claims` table because it contains both the settlement amount used for comparison and the claim start date: `FROM Claims`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Calculate the average settled amount across all claims with the aggregate expression: `avg(Amount_Settled)`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Place that aggregate in a scalar subquery so it can serve as the benchmark for each claim: `( SELECT avg(Amount_Settled) FROM Claims )`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep claims whose settled amount is equal to or below the computed average: `WHERE Amount_Settled <= ( SELECT avg(Amount_Settled) FROM Claims )`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the claim start date for every qualifying record in the outer query: `SELECT Date_Claim_Made`.

Question:
Find the full name of employee who supported the most number of customers.
answer: SELECT T1.first_name , T1.last_name FROM employees AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.support_rep_id GROUP BY T1.id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the employee records and assign the alias used for employee names and identifiers: `FROM employees AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each employee to the customers they support by matching the employee ID to the customer's support representative ID: `JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.support_rep_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined customer records by employee so that each employee's supported customers can be counted together: `GROUP BY T1.id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank employees by their customer count from highest to lowest and retain only the top employee: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the first and last name of the highest-ranked employee using the projection: `SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name`.

Question:
Which employee manage most number of peoples? List employee's first and last name, and number of people report to that employee.
answer: SELECT T2.first_name , T2.last_name ,  count(T1.reports_to) FROM employees AS T1 JOIN employees AS T2 ON T1.reports_to = T2.id GROUP BY T1.reports_to ORDER BY count(T1.reports_to) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Treat `employees` as both the reporting employees (`T1`) and their managers (`T2`), linking each employee’s `reports_to` value to the manager’s `id`: `FROM employees AS T1 JOIN employees AS T2 ON T1.reports_to = T2.id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Create one group for each manager so the employees reporting to the same person can be counted together: `GROUP BY T1.reports_to`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Count the reporting employees in each manager’s group using the non-null manager reference: `count(T1.reports_to)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank managers from the largest report count to the smallest and retain only the top manager: `ORDER BY count(T1.reports_to) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the manager’s first and last name together with the number of people managed: `SELECT T2.first_name , T2.last_name , count(T1.reports_to)`.

How many orders does Lucas Mancini has?
answer: SELECT count(*) FROM customers AS T1 JOIN invoices AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.customer_id WHERE T1.first_name = "Lucas" AND T1.last_name = "Mancini";

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the customer records so the requested person can be identified by name: `FROM customers AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each customer to their orders in `invoices` using the customer identifier: `JOIN invoices AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to customers whose first name is Lucas: `WHERE T1.first_name = "Lucas"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Complete the customer identification by also matching the last name Mancini: `AND T1.last_name = "Mancini"`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count all invoice rows remaining for that customer in the projection: `SELECT count(*)`.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each genre to its tracks by matching the genre primary key with the track’s genre reference: `JOIN tracks AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.genre_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the genre whose name is Rock: `WHERE T1.name = "Rock"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Use the track alias `T2` to reference the requested track-name column: `T2.name`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project only the track names by placing this SELECT clause before the joined tables and Rock filter: `SELECT T2.name`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Count the joined rows within each album group to determine its number of tracks: `count(T1.id)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only album groups whose track count is greater than 10: `HAVING count(T1.id) > 10`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the title of every album that satisfies the grouped track-count condition: `SELECT T1.title`.

Question:
List the name of playlist which has number of tracks greater than 100.
answer: SELECT T2.name FROM playlist_tracks AS T1 JOIN playlists AS T2 ON T2.id = T1.playlist_id GROUP BY T1.playlist_id HAVING count(T1.track_id)  >  100;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Begin with the junction table that records each track assigned to each playlist: `FROM playlist_tracks AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the playlist details so each playlist identifier can be associated with its name: `JOIN playlists AS T2 ON T2.id = T1.playlist_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by playlist so its track records can be counted together: `GROUP BY T1.playlist_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Retain only playlist groups whose track count is greater than 100: `HAVING count(T1.track_id) > 100`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the name of each qualifying playlist in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T2.name`.

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from `tracks`, since the requested output is track names, and connect each track to its purchase line using the track identifier: `FROM tracks AS T1 JOIN invoice_lines AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.track_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each purchased line to the invoice that contains it through the invoice identifier: `JOIN invoices AS T3 ON T3.id = T2.invoice_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Connect each invoice to the customer who made the purchase using the customer identifier: `JOIN customers AS T4 ON T4.id = T3.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined purchase records to the customer whose first and last names are Daan Peeters: `WHERE T4.first_name = "Daan" AND T4.last_name = "Peeters"`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the name of every track found through this customer’s invoice lines: `SELECT T1.name`.
